story: Asked why the penalty for petty theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could think of nothing worse for the large ones. Athenians said his laws were written in blood rather than ink.
Two women each claimed the same baby. Solomon called for a sword and offered them half each. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.
From Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled from the tribe to a kingdom to a Roman province, and from there into the words Judaism and Jewish.
Aaron was Moses's brother and did the talking, because Moses said he was slow of speech. The priesthood descended from him, so the family that spoke for Moses ended up speaking for everybody.

Careful — this is the Moses word, meaning of his law. The mosaic made of coloured tiles is unrelated: that one comes from the Muses, via rooms decorated in their honour. Two identical English words, two different origins.
David was a shepherd boy who became king, and the line descending from him mattered enormously to later writers — both Gospel genealogies take care to route Jesus back to him.

The giant loses because David refuses to fight the way giants fight. He turns down armour, keeps his sling, and wins at a distance — which makes the story less about size than about choosing your own contest.

Job loses his family, his wealth and his health, and keeps asking why. The book never really answers him. The patience of Job is proverbial, though anyone who reads it notices he complains a great deal.
Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later, almost nobody names a child Judas.

The point of the parable is who the helper was: Samaritans and Judeans despised each other. A modern retelling would have to pick whichever group the listener likes least, which is uncomfortable, and deliberate.

Arnold was one of the ablest American generals of the Revolution before he changed sides. There is a monument at Saratoga to his wounded leg — a boot, with no name on it, honouring the part of him that stayed loyal.
There is no balcony in Shakespeare's text. Juliet appears at a window; the word never occurs in the play. The balcony was added by an eighteenth-century adaptation and has been there ever since.

Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature — the monster has no name at all. Mary Shelley was eighteen when she wrote it, during a wet summer holiday where the group agreed to each write a ghost story.

Mercator put a picture of Atlas holding up the world on the front of his collection of maps in 1595, and the name transferred from the picture to the book. Atlas himself held up the sky, not the Earth.
His mother dipped him in the river Styx holding him by the heel, and that one patch stayed dry. Homer never mentions this — the heel appears in later versions, long after the Iliad.

Daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them. Her sister Panacea handled cures. Prevention and treatment, split between two sisters, which is roughly how medicine still divides.
The gentle death, as opposed to violent death, who was his brother. Freud later borrowed the name for a supposed drive toward destruction — a use the Greeks would not have recognised at all.
The Titans were the generation of gods before the Olympians, and they lost. Naming the largest ship afloat after a family famous chiefly for being overthrown was, in hindsight, an odd choice.
Mount Olympus was where the gods lived; Olympia, where the games were held, is a different place about two hundred miles away. English uses Olympian for both the majestic sense and the athletic one.

The river was named by a Spanish explorer who reported being attacked by women warriors. The bookshop was named after the river, because its founder wanted something that suggested enormous scale and started with A.
Spartan boys left home at seven for military training and were underfed on purpose, so they would learn to steal food. A boy caught stealing was punished — not for the theft, but for being caught.

Corinth was rich, and its architecture showed it. In Victorian England a Corinthian also meant a wealthy amateur sportsman — which is why an English football club founded by gentlemen amateurs is called Corinthian.
The order with the scrolls at the top, like a ram's horns or a rolled scroll. Greek writers considered it the feminine order to the Doric's masculine — slimmer, more decorated, and set on a base.
The plain one — no base, no scrolls, just fluting and a flat top. The Parthenon is Doric. It is the oldest of the three orders and the one that looks most like a stone version of a wooden post.

The most decorated of the three, with carved acanthus leaves. The story goes that a sculptor saw a basket left on a girl's grave with an acanthus plant growing up around it, and built a column out of the image.
The Eastern Roman Empire ran for a thousand years after Rome fell, with a court so layered in ceremony and intrigue that its name became the English word for anything needlessly complicated.

The Philistines were a real people with cities, pottery and trade. Matthew Arnold popularised the cultural insult in the 1860s, aiming it at the English middle classes — so an ancient nation is now a synonym for bad taste.
The famous dish was black broth — pork boiled in blood and vinegar. A visitor from another city tried it and said he now understood why Spartans were so willing to die in battle.
The oracle told Croesus that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Delphic answers were always true and almost never useful.
Pyrrhus beat the Romans twice and lost so many men doing it that he reportedly said one more such victory and we are undone. Rome could replace its losses; he could not.
Philip of Macedon warned Sparta that if he entered Laconia he would raze it to the ground. The Spartans sent back a one-word reply: If. He did not invade.
A medieval story held that a piece of the forbidden fruit stuck in Adam's throat and left a lump in every man since. The Bible never says the fruit was an apple either — that came from a Latin pun.
Adam simply means man or earth in Hebrew — he is named after the ground he was made from. Adamic language means the supposed original speech of humanity, before Babel scattered it.

After the flood, the covenant with Noah is made with all humanity rather than one people, and the rainbow is its sign. Flood stories appear across Mesopotamian literature, including one a thousand years older.
Judaism, Christianity and Islam all trace themselves to Abraham, which is why they are grouped under his name. It is one of the few labels all three traditions accept.

Raised after four days in the tomb. The name is now used for anything that comes back when it should not: Lazarus taxa in biology are species that reappear in the fossil record long after apparently going extinct.
Thomas said he would not believe without putting his hand in the wounds. He is remembered for the doubt rather than for what he did next, which was to believe immediately once he was shown.
Prodigal means wastefully extravagant, not returning — the son is prodigal in the first half of the parable, before he comes home. People use it to mean the coming back, which is exactly backwards.

Mary Magdalene was identified with a penitent sinner by a pope in 591, on no textual basis, and the Church formally separated them again in 1969. Her name also gave English maudlin — from paintings of her weeping.

The Pharisees were a reform movement that made scripture accessible outside the Temple, and rabbinic Judaism descends from them. The English insult comes entirely from how the Gospels portray their arguments.

The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, and they rejected any belief in resurrection. When the Temple was destroyed in AD 70 they vanished with it, leaving the Pharisees to shape everything that came after.

Babylon really did have the scale the legends suggest — walls, ziggurats, and possibly gardens. Its reputation for decadence comes mostly from the people it conquered, who had every reason to be unkind.

The Babylonians called their city bab-ilu, gate of the god. Hebrew writers heard it as balal, to confuse, and built the story of the scattered languages around the pun. The tower was probably a real ziggurat.
One family name became the word for supreme ruler in half of Europe, and outlasted the empire by fifteen centuries. Caesar himself was never emperor — the title did not exist yet when he was killed.

German emperors were Kaisers right up to 1918, and the word is Caesar worn down by two thousand years of German mouths. The pronunciation is actually closer to the original Latin than the English Caesar is.

Russian rulers took the same Roman title, arguing that after Constantinople fell Moscow was the third Rome. English still uses it for anyone put in charge of a problem — a drugs tsar, a productivity tsar.
Caesar's reform in 45 BC required one transitional year of 445 days to drag the calendar back into line with the seasons. Romans called it the year of confusion.
By 1582 the Julian year was ten days out of step, so October simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752 and had to skip eleven.
Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult. After Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack him head-on, it became a compliment, and Fabian has meant winning by patience ever since.

Given absolute power to save Rome, Cincinnatus won the war in about a fortnight, resigned, and went back to his farm. George Washington was compared to him constantly — and an American city is named for the society that admired him.

Pyrrho argued you should suspend judgement about everything, since certainty is not available. Sceptics after him used his name. He is not the Pyrrhus of the costly victory — two different Greeks, frequently confused.

Named after a painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught. The core claim is that you control your own judgements and nothing else — and two of its greatest writers were an enslaved man and a Roman emperor.

From the Greek for dog-like, meant as an insult about living rough in public. The Cynics accepted it. Their point was that convention is arbitrary; modern cynicism, assuming everyone is selfish, is a much later invention.

The Sophists were paid teachers of rhetoric in a city where winning an argument in court could save your life. Plato disliked them intensely, wrote the dialogues that survived, and their name has been an insult ever since.
Socrates claimed to know nothing and asked questions until the other person found the hole in their own answer. Athens executed him for it, which suggests the method works better than it is welcomed.

Euclid's fifth postulate, about parallel lines, bothered mathematicians for two thousand years because it looked like it should be provable. It is not — and dropping it produces the curved geometries relativity needs.

A spiral inside a tube: turn it and water climbs uphill. It is still used to move water and grain today, and versions have been found that predate Archimedes — he may have described it rather than invented it.

Babylonian tablets show the relationship a thousand years before Pythagoras. What his followers may have supplied is the proof — the argument that it must hold for every right triangle, not just the ones anyone measured.

Cross out every multiple of two, then of three, and keep going; what survives are the primes. The same man measured the circumference of the Earth using shadows in two cities and got within a few per cent.

Keep replacing the larger number with the remainder until nothing is left over. It is the oldest algorithm still in daily use, and a version of it runs every time your browser sets up an encrypted connection.

First, do no harm is not in it. That phrase comes from another of his works entirely. The actual oath swears by Apollo and includes clauses about not using a knife, which modern surgeons have quietly set aside.

Hippocrates described the sunken, drawn appearance of a face in the last stage of illness so precisely that the description was still being used two thousand years later, before machines could measure anything.

Galen dissected pigs and apes because Roman law forbade human dissection, then described human anatomy from what he found. His errors went uncorrected for fourteen hundred years, because questioning Galen was unthinkable.
Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was the standard European medical textbook for six centuries — longer than it was used in the world that produced it. He wrote it in Persia around 1025.

Vesalius dissected human bodies himself rather than lecturing while an assistant did the cutting, and found more than two hundred places where Galen was wrong. He published at twenty-eight and was attacked for it immediately.

Harvey proved blood circulates by simple arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in an hour than the whole body contains, so it cannot be constantly made and consumed. It must go round. His practice suffered for saying so.

Lister sprayed carbolic acid in operating theatres and death rates collapsed. Surgeons resented the implication that they carried infection on their own hands, and adoption took years longer than the evidence warranted.
The tremor Parkinson described is at its worst at rest and eases when the hand does something — the reverse of most tremors. That detail is still one of the first things a neurologist looks for.
The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story travelled west from Phoenicia. So calling a handsome man an Adonis is a compliment in a language almost nobody using it knows.
From al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician of the ninth century. His name latinised to Algoritmi. Another of his book titles gave English a second word — al-jabr became algebra.

Ampere founded the study of electromagnetism in a few weeks of intense work after hearing that a current deflects a compass needle. His father had been guillotined during the Revolution when he was eighteen.

skip_why: adult sense; excluded from kid-facing cards
story: From Aphrodite, Greek goddess of love. Substances have been claimed to have this effect for millennia, with very little evidence behind any of them.

Louis Braille was blinded at three by an accident in his father's workshop. At fifteen he adapted a military code for reading messages in the dark into a six-dot alphabet. His school did not adopt it until after his death.
Celsius put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing — the exact reverse of today's scale. It was flipped after he died, so the version everyone uses is upside down from the one he proposed.

Nicolas Chauvin was supposedly a soldier so devoted to Napoleon that he stayed loyal after everyone else gave up. Historians have never found evidence he existed. The word may be named after a man who was never born.

Doppler predicted the effect using starlight in 1842. Three years later a Dutch scientist tested it by hiring a train, filling an open carriage with trumpeters, and posting musicians along the track to write down what they heard.

Fahrenheit set zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably reproduce — a mix of ice, water and salt. That is why the landmarks look arbitrary: they were pinned to what he could make in a bucket.

Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch with electricity and concluded animals carry their own vital force. Volta disagreed, and invented the battery to prove it. Galvani was wrong, and English kept his name anyway.

McAdam worked out that a road needs no heavy stone foundation if it is raised, drained, and surfaced with small angular stones that lock together under traffic. Add tar to keep the dust down and you get tarmac.

Jean Martinet drilled Louis XIV's infantry into the best in Europe and was loathed for it. He was killed at the siege of Duisburg in 1672 by his own side's artillery, which some of his troops are said to have found fitting.

Mausolus ruled a small kingdom and his widow built him a tomb so vast it became one of the Seven Wonders. It stood for sixteen centuries, was destroyed by earthquakes, and its stone was carted off to build a castle.

Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

Panacea and Hygieia were sisters, daughters of the god of medicine — one the cure for everything, the other the prevention. English kept both, and uses panacea almost entirely to say that no such thing exists.

The Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread so he could keep working — or keep gambling, depending on who is telling it. The gambling version comes from a political opponent, so it may be an insult that stuck.

Adolphe Sax survived falling from a third floor, swallowing a pin, drinking acid by mistake and a gunpowder explosion, all before adulthood. His mother said he was a child doomed to misfortune. He invented the saxophone at thirty.
Homer says the herald Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together. In one version he challenges a god to a shouting match, loses, and dies of it — which is a very specific way to go.
Sybaris was so wealthy that its citizens were said to have banned noisy trades from the city so nobody's sleep was disturbed. A rival city destroyed it in 510 BC and diverted a river over the ruins.

Tesla claimed to see detailed visions of his inventions before building them, and tested some purely in his head. He died in a New York hotel room, owing money, having given away most of the patents that made others rich.

Watt did not invent the steam engine — he made an existing one three times more efficient by adding a separate condenser. He also coined horsepower, as a sales device to explain his engines to people who owned horses.

Count Zeppelin was fifty-two and retired when he started building airships. The Hindenburg disaster ended the industry in thirty-seven seconds of newsreel — and a British rock band took the name a generation later.
